chunks: SoC applications. The question: What are its applications?

A system on chip ("What is a system on chip") is a whole small computer on one piece of silicon, and you find one inside nearly every electronic product: phones, watches, cars, routers, cameras and tiny sensors.
The idea is the same everywhere. What changes is the main limit of each product, such as battery, heat, safety or speed, and that limit decides which blocks go on the chip.
Think of packing a backpack. For a day hike you take little and travel light. For a month-long expedition you take much more, but you have to carry it.
The weight you can carry is the limit, and it decides what you pack. A chip works the same way. The power it may use decides which blocks it gets.
The picture is incomplete in one way: chips also have a heat limit, and a backpack has no such limit.
Each line is life = energy / power. To get years from a coin cell the average power has to be in tens of microwatts, which is why IoT SoCs spend over 99% of time in deep sleep.
A phone has about 13x more energy than a watch but its SoC draws 100x more power on average, so it lasts hours rather than days.
Average power: total energy used divided by time, counting the idle moments too. Battery life: stored energy divided by average power.
Sleep current: the small current a chip draws while it waits and does nothing.
Accelerator: a block built for one job, like decoding video, that uses far less energy than a general processor doing the same job.
Throttling: slowing the chip down so it does not get too hot. Functional safety: designing so that faults are caught before they can hurt people, which matters in cars.
A coin cell battery stores about 0. 675 watt-hours (Wh) of energy. A sensor chip that averages 30 microwatts lasts 0. 675 over 0. 00003 equals 22 500 hours, about 2.
6 years in an ideal case. A phone battery stores 15. 4 watt hours. At an average of 1. 5 watts it lasts about 10 hours.
The formula is the same, but the power is 50,000 times different, so the chips look very different. That is the whole idea.
"SoCs power phones and tablets, wearables, IoT sensor nodes, laptops and consoles, cars, networking gear, smart TVs, cameras, drones and industrial controllers.

The architecture is the same, but the mix of blocks and the constraint differ: phones are limited by battery and heat, sensor nodes by microamps of sleep current, cars by safety and temperature range, routers by throughput.
Integration is what makes the small, low-power, low-cost versions possible."
